fatal_errors: The hypothesis does not predict coercivity above 100 Oe and therefore does not actually satisfy the central design objective.
The cited evidence concerns Al-containing B2/BCC alloys rather than fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti/C14 systems and does not support Ti-rich C14 precipitation or the proposed coercivity mechanism.

The proposed nonmagnetic-barrier/orbital-unquenching mechanism misses the target mechanism involving magnetic C14/fcc coexistence, Ti-transition-metal antiparallel coupling, spin canting, and domain-wall pinning.
The arbitrary 5-15 at.% Ti boundary conflicts with the substantially higher Ti content of the target equiatomic and C14-dominant compositions.
explanation: The response partially reconstructs the useful design concept by proposing a Ti-rich C14 Laves secondary phase within an fcc matrix and by suggesting a single-phase versus dual-phase comparison with structural verification. Its falsification experiment could establish whether secondary phases correlate with coercivity. However, it replaces the as-cast, rapidly quenched equiatomic dual-phase alloy and compositionally matched C14-dominant control with an unspecified precipitation heat treatment. It gives no affirmative or quantitative high-coercivity prediction, omits the approximately 667 Oe result at 400 K and the multiple magnetic transitions, and does not reconstruct the antiferromagnetic sublattice coupling or electronic-structure evidence. The baseline is also overstated as below 10 Oe rather than the relevant sub-100 Oe limitation. Most importantly, the supplied citations are compositionally and structurally irrelevant, so the central materials and mechanistic claims lack valid evidentiary support.
